It’s Hard to Protect Your Nest Egg from Nvidia
 
Plus, Nvidia’s royal family, and souring apartment deals
 

Good morning, I’m filling in for Spencer Jakab. Futures are pointing to another down day for stocks, in particular tech heavyweights. Sharp losses Monday extended to global markets as investors await quarterly results after the bell today from Nvidia. The focus for investors will be on life after Jensen Huang, his Chinese spy scandal and the impact of a crackdown on chip exports to China. Perhaps an even bigger concern: whether Nvidia now will rein in its aggressive dealmaking and support of the AI ecosystem.

 

​📈 Follow our live markets data and coverage.

It’s everywhere

 

Many investors have been fleeing Nvidia’s stock over the past month. But for anyone with retirement accounts or fund investments, escaping the AI chip giant isn’t easy.

 

Nvidia’s runaway AI success was so large it came to account for 8.9% of the S&P 500’s valuation at its peak in May. It has since fallen to about 6%, but still makes up a large slice of U.S. stock index funds.

 

What’s more, Nvidia’s size and role as an AI champion made it a tempting choice for many fund managers looking to add some oomph to their returns.

 

The result is that Nvidia is pervasive in portfolios at a time when many investors are worried about their exposure. The company’s sex-and-spying scandal led to CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster last week. Fears of the AI trade slowing or collapsing have been heightened.

 

The stock’s prevalence may also help explain why investors appear hesitant to swoop in on what, by many valuation metrics, is a stock-market bargain. They aren’t keen to load up on more of what they probably already have.

 

Nvidia’s stock takes up a surprising chunk of many mutual-fund portfolios, even those that appear defensive. It was, for example, about 8.5% of Fidelity’s Dividend Growth Fund at the end of October, despite having one of the lower dividend payout ratios in the S&P 500. Lots of other dividend-focused funds feature it, too, from JPMorgan’s Dividend Leaders ETF to Invesco’s Dividend Income Fund, both of which had roughly 2% allocated.

 

While Nvidia upped its dividend earlier this year, the company mainly returns money to investors via share buybacks. In September, it raised authorized buybacks through the 2028 fiscal year to $230 billion. Nvidia’s dividend yield is about 0.5%, according to FactSet, roughly a third of the S&P 500’s 1.4%.

 

Nvidia also features widely in target-date retirement funds, even ones with expected retirement years now long past. Those funds have allocations to stock indexes through indirect mutual-fund holdings. That means exposure to Nvidia.

 

To some degree, this makes sense. Nvidia is a big part of indexes, so investors should expect to hold it when they buy them. A dividend-growth portfolio manager might justify a holding by factoring in the company’s buybacks and the likelihood it will raise dividends in the future.

 

But there is some degree of choice involved, too. T. Rowe Price’s Dividend Growth Fund had just 1.1% of its portfolio allocated to Nvidia at the end of September—far lower than Fidelity’s competing fund.

 

The addiction to Nvidia has become so strong that a quarter of stock funds had some exposure, according to Morningstar, underlining how hard it is for investors to stay away.

 

Nvidia’s board quickly parted ways with Jensen Huang after he admitted to an affair with a woman suspected of feeding intelligence to China. For investors who want to disentangle themselves, it might take much longer.

Stocks I’m Watching

 

↘️ Alibaba, Baidu: New York-listed depositary receipts in Chinese tech names took a hit premarket, following a fresh U.S. move to crack down on chip exports to China.

 

↘️ Intel: That same news rocked U.S. AI stocks yesterday, and the selloff continued in premarket trading today. Intel was among the biggest losers as investors worried about falling demand for chips.

 

↗️ Lennar: Even without Warren Buffett, the touch of Berkshire Hathaway can move a stock. Lennar ticked up in thin premarket trading after Berkshire upped its stake in the house builder.

 

↘️ Deutsche Bank: Shares in Germany’s largest lender fell following reports of bad behavior across multiple media outlets. DB said the reports, which are based on millions of leaked internal documents, refer to years-old matters, and that it’s a different bank today.

 

🔎 Walt Disney: The entertainment group reports earnings ahead of market open.
